title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: Nothing is more painful to the human mind than the dead calm that follows after emotions have been whipped up by a rapid series of events — a stillness that robs the soul of both hope and fear. Justine was dead. She was at rest. But I was alive. Blood flowed freely through my veins, yet a crushing weight of despair and remorse sat on my heart that nothing could lift. Sleep fled from me. I wandered like an evil spirit, for I had committed deeds of indescribable horror — and more, much more, I was sure, was yet to come. Yet my heart overflowed with kindness and a love of virtue. I'd begun life with good intentions and longed for the moment when I could put them into practice and be useful to others. Now all was destroyed. Instead of the clear conscience that had once let me look back with satisfaction and look forward with hope, I was gripped by guilt and remorse that dragged me into a hell of torment beyond what language can express.

This mental state ate away at my health, which had perhaps never fully recovered from its first collapse. I avoided other people. Any sound of joy or contentment was torture to me. Solitude was my only comfort — deep, dark, deathlike solitude.

My father noticed the change in my mood and habits with pain. Drawing on the feelings of his own clear conscience and blameless life, he tried to give me strength and to awaken the courage to drive away the dark cloud hanging over me. "Victor," he said, "do you think I don't suffer too? No one could love a child more than I loved your brother" — tears came to his eyes — "but isn't it our duty to the survivors not to add to their unhappiness by a show of excessive grief? It's also a duty you owe yourself, for excessive sorrow prevents improvement or enjoyment, or even the ability to fulfill daily duties. Without that, no man is fit for society."

This advice, though good, didn't apply to my situation at all. I should have been the first to hide my grief and comfort my friends — if remorse hadn't mixed its bitterness, and terror its alarm, with everything else I felt. All I could do was look at my father in despair and try to hide from his sight.

Around this time, we moved to our house at Belrive. This change was especially welcome to me. Geneva's gates shut regularly at ten, and it was impossible to stay out on the lake after that hour, so living within the city walls had become unbearable to me. Now I was free. Often, after the rest of the family had gone to bed, I took the boat and spent hours on the water. Sometimes the wind filled my sails and carried me along. Sometimes I rowed to the middle of the lake, then let the boat drift while I gave in to my miserable thoughts. I was often tempted — when all around me was peaceful and I was the only restless creature wandering through such beauty, except perhaps a bat or the frogs whose harsh croaking I heard only near the shore — I was often tempted to plunge into the silent lake, to let the water close over me and my suffering forever. But I held back. I thought of Elizabeth, so heroic and so full of suffering, whom I loved dearly and whose life was bound to mine. I thought of my father and surviving brother. Should I desert them through cowardice and leave them exposed and unprotected against the malice of the fiend I'd let loose among them?

In those moments I wept bitterly and wished for peace — if only so I could bring comfort and happiness to my family. But that was impossible. Remorse destroyed every hope. I had caused irreversible evil, and I lived in daily fear that the monster I had created would commit some new atrocity. I had a vague feeling that it wasn't over — that he would still commit some monstrous crime that would almost erase the memory of what had come before. As long as anyone I loved still lived, there was always room for fear. My hatred of this fiend was beyond description. When I thought of him, I gnashed my teeth, my eyes burned, and I wished desperately to destroy the life I had so thoughtlessly given. When I considered his crimes and malice, my hatred and desire for revenge burst all bounds. I would have made a pilgrimage to the highest peak of the Andes if I could have thrown him from the summit. I longed to see him again so I could unleash the full force of my hatred and avenge the deaths of William and Justine.

Ours was a house of mourning. My father's health was deeply shaken by recent events. Elizabeth was sad and despairing. She no longer took pleasure in her usual occupations. All enjoyment seemed wrong, a sin against the dead. Endless tears and grief, she felt, were the only fitting tribute to innocence so cruelly destroyed. She was no longer the happy girl who had once walked with me along the lake, talking excitedly about our future. The first of those sorrows that are sent to wean us from this world had reached her, and its shadow had dimmed her brightest smiles.

"When I think, dear cousin," she said, "about the miserable death of Justine Moritz, I no longer see the world as I used to. Before, I read about vice and injustice in books or heard about it from others, and it seemed like ancient history or imaginary evil — remote and more real to my reason than to my feelings. But now misery has come home. People seem to me like monsters thirsting for each other's blood. Yet I know I'm being unfair. Everyone believed that poor girl was guilty. If she had committed the crime, she would have been the most depraved creature alive. To have murdered the son of her benefactor — a child she'd nursed from birth and seemed to love as her own — for a few jewels! I couldn't consent to anyone's death, but I would certainly have thought such a person unfit to live among others. But she was innocent. I know it. I feel it. You agree with me, which confirms what I know. Alas! Victor, when lies can look so much like truth, who can feel certain of happiness? I feel as if I'm walking on the edge of a cliff, with thousands pushing me toward the abyss. William and Justine were killed, and the murderer walks free — perhaps even respected. But even if I were condemned to the scaffold for the same crimes, I wouldn't trade places with such a wretch."

I listened to this with the most extreme anguish. I — not directly, but in effect — was the true murderer. Elizabeth read the anguish on my face and, gently taking my hand, said, "My dearest friend, you must calm yourself. These events have affected me deeply, God knows. But I'm not as wretched as you are. There's an expression of despair — and sometimes revenge — in your face that frightens me. Dear Victor, drive away these dark passions. Remember the friends who love you and center all their hopes on you. Have we lost the power to make you happy? Ah! While we love each other, while we remain true to each other, here in this land of peace and beauty — your native country — we can enjoy every blessing. What can disturb our peace?"

And couldn't such words, from the person I treasured above all others, be enough to drive away the fiend lurking in my heart? Even as she spoke, I drew close to her, as if in terror, afraid the destroyer might be near to snatch her from me at that very moment.

So neither the tenderness of friendship, nor the beauty of earth or sky, could save my soul from suffering. Even the words of love were powerless. I was enveloped in a cloud that no good influence could penetrate. The wounded deer dragging its dying limbs to some hidden thicket, there to stare at the arrow that pierced it and die — that was my image.

Sometimes I could cope with the sullen despair that overwhelmed me. But sometimes the storm of passions in my soul drove me to seek relief through physical exercise and change of scenery. It was during one of these fits that I suddenly left home and headed toward the nearby Alpine valleys. In the magnificence and permanence of those scenes, I hoped to forget myself and my sorrows, which were fleeting because they were human. My wanderings took me toward the valley of Chamounix. I'd visited it often as a boy. Six years had passed since then. _I_ was a wreck, but nothing had changed in those savage, enduring landscapes.

I traveled the first part of the journey on horseback, then hired a mule as more sure-footed on these rough mountain roads. The weather was fine. It was about the middle of August, nearly two months after Justine's death — that miserable turning point from which I dated all my suffering. The weight on my spirit lightened as I plunged deeper into the gorge of the Arve. The immense mountains and cliffs that towered over me on every side, the sound of the river crashing among rocks, the roar of waterfalls — all spoke of a power as mighty as God himself. I stopped fearing or bowing before anything less than the force that had created and ruled these elements, here displayed in their most terrifying form. Still, as I climbed higher, the valley grew more magnificent. Ruined castles clinging to the cliffs of pine-covered mountains, the wild Arve river, cottages peeking out among the trees — all formed a scene of extraordinary beauty. But the scene was heightened and made sublime by the mighty Alps, their white, shining peaks and domes towering above everything as if they belonged to another earth, the home of another race of beings.

I crossed the bridge at Pélissier, where the river gorge opened before me, and began ascending the mountain above it. Soon I entered the valley of Chamounix — more wonderful and sublime than the valley of Servox I'd just passed through, but not as beautiful or picturesque. The high, snowy mountains formed its immediate boundaries. I saw no more ruined castles or fertile fields. Immense glaciers came right to the road. I heard the rumbling thunder of falling avalanches and saw the smoke of their passage. Mont Blanc — supreme and magnificent — rose from the surrounding peaks, its tremendous dome overlooking the valley.

A tingling, long-lost sense of pleasure often came over me during this journey. Some turn in the road, some sudden new sight, reminded me of days gone by and was linked to the lighthearted joy of boyhood. The very winds seemed to whisper comfort, and mother Nature told me to weep no more. Then the kind spell would break, and I'd find myself chained to grief again, wallowing in all the misery of reflection. Then I'd spur my animal on, trying to forget the world, my fears, and above all myself — or, more desperately, I'd dismount and throw myself on the grass, crushed by horror and despair.

At last I reached the village of Chamounix. Extreme exhaustion of both body and mind overcame me. For a short time I stood at the window, watching pale lightning flicker above Mont Blanc and listening to the rush of the Arve flowing noisily below. These same soothing sounds acted as a lullaby to my overwrought senses. When I put my head on the pillow, sleep crept over me. I felt it come and blessed the giver of oblivion.
